::: {.solutions}

**19 questions.** Suggested time: **80 minutes**, no calculator.

Every question comes from a TMUA past paper, a TMUA mock or the official Notes on Logic and Proof, and its source
is shown beside the question number. None of them appears in the S4 class questions.

For every question the routine is the same: **write the statement as a chain of quantifiers, decide who is chosen
first, then settle it** — one example proves a "there exists" or breaks a "for all", and anything else needs an
argument covering every case. To negate, **flip every quantifier in order, then negate the inside.**

| Section | What it covers | Questions |
|---|---|---|
| **A — Reading for all and there exists** | truth of quantified statements, and the order of quantifiers | 1–5 |
| **B — Negating a definition** | negating quantifier chains, and counterexamples to nested statements | 6–8 |
| **C — What "for every" forces** | using a "for all" condition on a region, a constant or a selection | 9–13 |
| **D — "For some" and "possible"** | hidden "there exists" statements: one witness to accept, a full argument to reject | 14–19 |

# Section A — Reading for all and there exists

## Question 1 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">Notes on Logic and Proof · Exercise M, Q1</span>

::: {.question}
Which of the following are true and which are false?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**i.** **for every** real $x$, $x^2$ is rational

&nbsp;&nbsp;**ii.** **there exists** a real $x$ such that $x^2$ is rational

&nbsp;&nbsp;**iii.** **for every** real $x$, $x^2>x$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**iv.** **there exists** a real $x$ such that $x^2>x$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**v.** **for every** real $x$, $x^3>0$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**vi.** **there exists** a real $x$ such that $x^3>0$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**vii.** **for every** real $x$ and $y$, $x^2+y^2>2xy$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**viii.** **there exists** real $x$ and $y$ such that $x^2+y^2>2xy$
:::

Which **one** of the following is true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** Statement $(*)$ is true for all values of $n$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** Statement $(*)$ is true for all values of $n$ which are odd, but not for any other values of $n$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** Statement $(*)$ is true for all values of $n$ which are multiples of $3$, but not for any other values of $n$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** Statement $(*)$ is true for all values of $n$ which are multiples of $6$, but not for any other values of $n$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** Statement $(*)$ is not true for any value of $n$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** I and IV only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** II and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** III and IV only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** None of the statements is true.

# Section B — Negating a definition

## Question 6 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">TMUA early specimen · P2 Q17</span>

::: {.question}
Let $S$ be a set of positive integers, for example $S$ could consist of $3$, $4$, and $8$.

A positive integer $n$ is called an $S$-number **if and only if** for every factor $m$ of $n$ with $m>1$, the number
$m$ is a multiple of some number in $S$.

So in the above example, $9$ is an $S$-number; this is because the factors of $9$ greater than $1$ are $3$ and $9$, and
each of these is a multiple of $3$.

Positive integer $n$ is therefore **not** an $S$-number **if and only if**

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** for **every** (positive) factor $m$ of $n$ with $m>1$, there is a number in $S$ which is not a factor of $m$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** for **every** (positive) factor $m$ of $n$ with $m>1$, there is no number in $S$ which is a factor of $m$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** for **every** (positive) factor $m$ of $n$ with $m>1$, every number in $S$ is a factor of $m$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** for **some** (positive) factor $m$ of $n$ with $m>1$, there is a number in $S$ which is not a factor of $m$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** for **some** (positive) factor $m$ of $n$ with $m>1$, there is no number in $S$ which is a factor of $m$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** for **some** (positive) factor $m$ of $n$ with $m>1$, every number in $S$ is a factor of $m$.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:7cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 7 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">JZ Maths Mock B · P2 Q15</span>

::: {.question}
A set $X$ of positive integers, with $\lvert X\rvert\ge3$, is called **cross-linked** if and only if for every number $x$ in
$X$ there exist two distinct numbers $y$ and $z$ in $X$, both different from $x$, and a prime $p$, such that $p$ divides
each of $x$, $y$ and $z$.

Let $Y$ be a set of positive integers with $\lvert Y\rvert\ge3$.

Which of the following statements is equivalent to $Y$ being **not** cross-linked?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** For every number $x$ in $Y$, and for every two distinct numbers $y$ and $z$ in $Y$ with $y\ne x$ and $z\ne x$, there is no prime which divides all of $x$, $y$ and $z$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** For every number $x$ in $Y$ there exist two distinct numbers $y$ and $z$ in $Y$, both different from $x$, such that no prime divides all of $x$, $y$ and $z$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** There exists a number $x$ in $Y$, and there exist two distinct numbers $y$ and $z$ in $Y$ with $y\ne x$ and $z\ne x$, such that no prime divides all of $x$, $y$ and $z$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** There exists a number $x$ in $Y$ such that for every two distinct numbers $y$ and $z$ in $Y$ with $y\ne x$ and $z\ne x$, there is no prime which divides all of $x$, $y$ and $z$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** There exists a number $x$ in $Y$ such that for every two distinct numbers $y$ and $z$ in $Y$ with $y\ne x$ and $z\ne x$, there is a prime which divides $x$ but divides neither $y$ nor $z$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** For every number $x$ in $Y$ there exist two distinct numbers $y$ and $z$ in $Y$, both different from $x$, and a prime $p$, such that $p$ divides $x$ but $p$ does not divide $y$ and $p$ does not divide $z$.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:8cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 8 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">JZ Maths Mock C · P2 Q12</span>

::: {.question}
A student makes the following claim:

> If $f$ is a real-valued function such that, for some constant $a$, $\;\dfrac{f(x)+f(-x)}{2}=a\;$ for all real values of $x$, then there exists a constant $k$ such that $f(x)=kx+a$ for all real values of $x$.

Examine their claim above, and determine which of the following is true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** The claim is true.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** $f(x)=2x+1$ is a counterexample to the claim.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** $f(x)=\sin x$ is a counterexample to the claim.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** $f(x)=\tan x$ is a counterexample to the claim.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** $f(x)=\cos x$ is a counterexample to the claim.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** $f(x)=-x$ is a counterexample to the claim.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:7cm"}
Working
:::

# Section C — What "for every" forces

## Question 9 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">JZ Maths Mock A · P2 Q10</span>

::: {.question}
The region $R$ in the $(x,y)$-plane consists of all points satisfying both

$$\lvert y-x^2\rvert<2\qquad\text{and}\qquad x+y<4 .$$

Which of the following claims about points in $R$ are true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I:** **For every** $(x,y)\in R$, $\;y\le6$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II:** **For every** $(x,y)\in R$, $\;y>-2$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III:** **For every** $(x,y)\in R$, $\;x\le2$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** None of them

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** I only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** I and II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** I and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** II and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** I, II and III
:::

# Section D — "For some" and "possible"

## Question 14 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2023 · P2 Q8</span>

::: {.question}
A student draws a triangle that is acute-angled or obtuse-angled but not right-angled.

The student counts the number of straight lines that divide the triangle into two triangles, at least one of which is
right-angled.

Which of the following statements is/are true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; The student can draw a triangle for which there is exactly $1$ such straight line.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; The student can draw a triangle for which there are exactly $2$ such straight lines.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** &nbsp; The student can draw a triangle for which there are exactly $3$ such straight lines.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none of them

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** I only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** I and II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** I and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** II and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** I, II and III
:::

## Question 15 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">JZ Maths Mock D · P2 Q8</span>

::: {.question}
Let $a$ be a real number with $a>1$, and let $f$ be a function such that

$$f(0)=1,\qquad f(2)>a^2,\qquad f(-1)<a^{-1}.$$

Consider the following four statements.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I.** $f(x)=b^x$ **for some** real number $b$ with $b>a$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II.** $f(x)=b^x$ **for some** real number $b$ with $0<b<a$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III.** $f(x)=a^{kx}$ **for some** real number $k$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**IV.** $f(x)=b^{x^2}$ **for some** positive real number $b$.

Which of the statements **might** be true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** Statement I only.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** Statement III only.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** Statements I and III only.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** Statements I, II and III only.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** Statements I, III and IV only.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** Statements II and IV only.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** Statements II, III and IV only.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** All four statements.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:8cm"}
Working

The student then attempts to draw a triangle $ABC$ with:

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; **For some** choice of $x$ and $y$, there are exactly **two** different triangles the student could draw.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** &nbsp; **For some** choice of $x$ and $y$, there are exactly **three** different triangles the student could draw.

(Note that congruent triangles are considered to be the same.)

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none of them

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** I only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** I and II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** I and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** II and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** I, II and III

&nbsp;&nbsp;**2** &nbsp; **For some** value of $c$: there is exactly one solution with $0\le x\le\pi$ **and** there are no solutions with $-\pi<x<0$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**3** &nbsp; **For some** value of $c$: there is exactly one solution with $0\le x\le\pi$ **and** there are no solutions with $x>\pi$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** 1 only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** 2 only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** 3 only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** 1 and 2 only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** 1 and 3 only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** 2 and 3 only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** 1, 2 and 3
:::

## Question 19 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">JZ Maths Mock E · P2 Q16</span>

::: {.question}
Let $f$ be a positive function defined on $[0,\infty)$ and twice differentiable on $(0,\infty)$. Define

$$I=\int_0^4f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x,$$

and let $J_n$ be the trapezium rule estimate of $I$ using $n$ strips of equal width, where $n$ is a positive integer.

Which of the following statements are **necessarily** true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(1)** If $f''(x)>0$ **for all** $0<x<4$, then $J_n>I$ **for every** positive integer $n$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(2)** If $f''(x)\ge0$ and $f'(x)>0$ **for all** $0<x<4$, then $J_{n+1}<J_n$ **for every** positive integer $n$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(3)** If $I<J_n$ **for some** positive integer $n$, then $\displaystyle\int_0^4f(4-x)\,\mathrm{d}x<J_{n+1}$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** (1) only.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** (2) only.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** (3) only.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** (1) and (2) only.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** (1) and (3) only.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** (2) and (3) only.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** none of them.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** all of them
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:9cm"}
Working
:::

:::
